options: gains are never worth the effort
effort and hardship are necessary to achieve success
questions.explanation: 'No pain, no gain' means that hard work and difficulty are necessary to achieve success.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
Once the fine was paid, the driver was finally off the hook.
The idiom 'off the hook' means:
options: unable to make a phone call
free from blame or an obligation
questions.explanation: 'Off the hook' means to be free from an obligation, blame, or difficult situation.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
The new employee was praised for always being on the ball during meetings.
The idiom 'on the ball' means:
questions.explanation: 'On the ball' means to be alert, competent, and quick to understand or respond to situations.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
He refused to choose a side and remained on the fence throughout the debate.
The idiom 'on the fence' means:
questions.explanation: 'On the fence' means undecided or unable to choose between two options.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
Once bitten, twice shy — after the last betrayal, she was cautious about trusting new partners.
The idiom 'once bitten, twice shy' means:
options: being cautious after a previous bad experience
questions.explanation: 'Once bitten, twice shy' means a bad experience makes a person more careful in the future.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
The news of his promotion came completely out of the blue.
The idiom 'out of the blue' means:
questions.explanation: 'Out of the blue' means something happens suddenly and unexpectedly.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
She was over the moon when she heard she had won the scholarship.
The idiom 'over the moon' means:
questions.explanation: 'Over the moon' means extremely happy or delighted.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
Getting stuck in traffic on a Monday morning is par for the course in this city.
The idiom 'par for the course' means:
options: typical or expected in a given situation
questions.explanation: 'Par for the course' means something that is typical or to be expected in a particular situation.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
Instead of solving the issue, the manager tried to pass the buck to his assistant.
The idiom 'pass the buck' means:
options: to shift responsibility or blame to someone else
questions.explanation: 'Pass the buck' means to shift blame or responsibility onto someone else.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
Realising his friend was pulling his leg, he finally laughed at the joke.
The idiom 'pull someone's leg' means:
options: to tease or joke with someone
questions.explanation: 'Pull someone's leg' means to tease someone by telling them something untrue as a joke.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
After the shocking news, it took him a while to pull himself together.
The idiom 'pull oneself together' means:
options: to regain control of one's emotions
questions.explanation: 'Pull yourself together' means to recover control of your emotions after being upset.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
Investing all his savings in one company, he put all his eggs in one basket.
The idiom 'put all your eggs in one basket' means:
options: to risk everything on a single plan or venture
questions.explanation: 'Put all your eggs in one basket' means to risk everything on the success of a single plan or venture.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
His sudden resignation rained on everyone's parade at the celebration dinner.
The idiom 'rain on someone's parade' means:
options: to spoil someone's plans or happiness
questions.explanation: 'Rain on someone's parade' means to spoil someone's plans or ruin their happy mood.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
A careful reader can read between the lines to understand the author's true message.
The idiom 'read between the lines' means:
options: to understand a hidden or implied meaning
to memorise a passage word for word
to skip parts of a text
questions.explanation: 'Read between the lines' means to understand the hidden meaning of something that is not directly stated.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
The name sounded familiar; it rang a bell, but she couldn't remember where she'd heard it.
The idiom 'ring a bell' means:
options: to signal the end of an event
questions.explanation: 'Ring a bell' means something sounds familiar, though you may not fully remember it.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
As a rule of thumb, you should always save a portion of your income.
The idiom 'rule of thumb' means:
questions.explanation: 'Rule of thumb' means a broadly accurate guide or principle based on practice rather than strict theory.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
She always saves a portion of her salary for a rainy day.
The idiom 'save for a rainy day' means:
options: to save money for a possible future need
questions.explanation: 'Save for a rainy day' means to save money for a time when it might be needed unexpectedly.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
After months of hardship, they could finally see the light at the end of the tunnel.
The idiom 'the light at the end of the tunnel' means:
options: a sign that a difficult situation is about to improve
questions.explanation: 'The light at the end of the tunnel' means a sign that a period of hardship is nearing its end.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
Unsure which side to support, the senator chose to sit on the fence.
The idiom 'sit on the fence' means:
options: to avoid taking a side in a dispute
questions.explanation: 'Sit on the fence' means to avoid making a decision or taking a side.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
Rather than answer immediately, she decided to sleep on it before giving her final decision.
The idiom 'sleep on it' means:
options: to delay a decision until the next day to think it over
questions.explanation: 'Sleep on it' means to postpone a decision until the next day in order to think about it further.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
Despite the setbacks, the results so far are so far so good.
The idiom 'so far so good' means:
options: things have gone badly from the start
things have gone well up to this point
questions.explanation: 'So far so good' means everything has proceeded successfully up to the present moment.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
His success in the interview really stole the thunder from the other candidates.
The idiom 'steal someone's thunder' means:
options: to take credit or attention away from someone else
questions.explanation: 'Steal someone's thunder' means to take attention or credit away from someone else's achievement.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
Despite criticism, the coach decided to stick to his guns about the new strategy.
The idiom 'stick to one's guns' means:
options: to maintain one's position despite pressure to change
to give up an argument quickly
to use a weapon in self-defence
questions.explanation: 'Stick to your guns' means to remain firm in your position or opinion despite opposition.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
The information came straight from the horse's mouth, so it must be true.
The idiom 'straight from the horse's mouth' means:
options: directly from the original or reliable source
questions.explanation: 'Straight from the horse's mouth' means information received directly from the person originally involved.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
It took the whole nine yards to organise the wedding, but it was worth it.
The idiom 'the whole nine yards' means:
questions.explanation: 'The whole nine yards' means everything included; the complete or full amount.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
After several failed attempts, the boxer decided to throw in the towel.
The idiom 'throw in the towel' means:
options: to give up or admit defeat
questions.explanation: 'Throw in the towel' means to give up or admit defeat, a term borrowed from boxing.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
After dating for five years, the couple finally decided to tie the knot.
The idiom 'tie the knot' means:
questions.explanation: 'Tie the knot' means to get married.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
Looking back at old photos, she realised how quickly time flies.
The idiom 'time flies' means:
questions.explanation: 'Time flies' means that time seems to pass very quickly.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
Some people prefer coffee and others tea; to each his own.
The idiom 'to each his own' means:
options: everyone has their own preferences, which should be respected
no one should have an opinion
everyone must follow the same rule
questions.explanation: 'To each his own' means everyone is entitled to their own tastes and opinions.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
The referee decided to turn a blind eye to the minor foul.
The idiom 'turn a blind eye' means:
questions.explanation: 'Turn a blind eye' means to deliberately ignore something you know is wrong.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
The small clinic operated under the radar for years before being noticed by regulators.
The idiom 'under the radar' means:
questions.explanation: 'Under the radar' means without being noticed.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
With the final decision still up in the air, no one knew what to expect.
The idiom 'up in the air' means:
questions.explanation: 'Up in the air' means uncertain or not yet decided.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
Even after the apology, some resentment remained like water under the bridge.
The idiom 'water under the bridge' means:
options: past events that are no longer worth worrying about
a physical location near a river
questions.explanation: 'Water under the bridge' means past problems or events that have been resolved and are no longer important.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
They say when it rains, it pours, since three problems occurred on the same day.
The idiom 'when it rains, it pours' means:
options: difficulties tend to occur all at once
questions.explanation: 'When it rains, it pours' means that when problems occur, they often happen all at the same time.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
It took him a while to wrap his head around the new tax policy.
The idiom 'wrap one's head around' means:
options: to fully understand a complicated idea
questions.explanation: 'Wrap your head around' means to come to understand something that is complex or confusing.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
The old, worn-out book turned out to be extremely valuable — you can't judge a book by its cover.
The idiom 'you can't judge a book by its cover' means:
options: a person or thing's true nature cannot be known from appearance alone
books should always be judged by their titles
covers are more important than content
questions.explanation: 'You can't judge a book by its cover' means you cannot know what someone or something is really like based on outward appearance.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
On cloud nine after the announcement, she could not stop smiling all day.
The idiom 'on cloud nine' means:
questions.explanation: 'On cloud nine' means to be extremely happy or elated.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
Frustrated with the delay, he decided to hit the road before traffic got worse.
The idiom 'hit the road' means:
questions.explanation: 'Hit the road' means to leave or start a journey.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
Repairing the roof after the storm will break the bank for most homeowners.
The idiom 'break the bank' means:
options: to save a great deal of money
questions.explanation: 'Break the bank' means to cost a great deal of money, more than one can afford.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
In a nutshell, the meeting was about budget cuts and new deadlines.
The idiom 'in a nutshell' means:
questions.explanation: 'In a nutshell' means to summarise something in the fewest possible words.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
The documentary about pollution gave the students plenty of food for thought.
The idiom 'food for thought' means:
questions.explanation: 'Food for thought' means something that is worth serious consideration.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
As the interview date approached, she began to get cold feet about the new job.
The idiom 'get cold feet' means:
options: to become nervous or hesitant about a plan
questions.explanation: 'Get cold feet' means to become nervous or lose confidence about doing something you had planned.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
He decided to go cold turkey and stop smoking immediately.
The idiom 'go cold turkey' means:
options: to stop a habit suddenly and completely
questions.explanation: 'Go cold turkey' means to stop doing something, especially a habit, suddenly and completely.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
Before the announcement, everyone was told to hold their horses and wait patiently.
The idiom 'hold your horses' means:
questions.explanation: 'Hold your horses' means to wait and be patient; don't act too hastily.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
She promised to keep her fingers crossed for his success in the exam.
The idiom 'keep your fingers crossed' means:
questions.explanation: 'Keep your fingers crossed' means to hope that something will happen the way you want.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
Despite the challenges, the couple managed to make ends meet every month.
The idiom 'make ends meet' means:
options: to earn just enough money to cover basic expenses
to earn far more money than needed
questions.explanation: 'Make ends meet' means to have just enough money to cover one's basic needs.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
The deal was agreed with no strings attached, meaning no hidden conditions.
The idiom 'no strings attached' means:
questions.explanation: 'No strings attached' means something is offered without conditions or obligations.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
After the long discussion, both teams were finally on the same page.
The idiom 'on the same page' means:
options: in agreement or having the same understanding
questions.explanation: 'On the same page' means people share the same understanding or opinion about something.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
After months of struggle, the small business was finally out of the woods.
The idiom 'out of the woods' means:
options: no longer in danger or difficulty
questions.explanation: 'Out of the woods' means to be safe after having been in a difficult or dangerous situation.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
Realising the plan would not work, the manager decided to pull the plug on the project.
The idiom 'pull the plug' means:
questions.explanation: 'Pull the plug' means to put a stop to a project or activity, often abruptly.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
The landlord finally decided to put his foot down about late rent payments.
The idiom 'put one's foot down' means:
options: to take a firm stand about something
questions.explanation: 'Put your foot down' means to take a firm stand or insist on something.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
The market was flooded because it had been raining cats and dogs all morning.
The idiom 'raining cats and dogs' means:
questions.explanation: 'Raining cats and dogs' means it is raining very heavily.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
By the final lap, the runner had begun to run out of steam.
The idiom 'run out of steam' means:
questions.explanation: 'Run out of steam' means to lose the energy or enthusiasm to continue doing something.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
The report helped shed light on the causes of the factory accident.
The idiom 'shed light on' means:
options: to make something clearer or easier to understand
to reduce the brightness of a room
questions.explanation: 'Shed light on' means to help explain or clarify something.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
Instead of taking the bull by the horns, he kept avoiding the difficult conversation.
The idiom 'take the bull by the horns' means:
options: to ask someone else for help
to confront a difficult situation directly and bravely
questions.explanation: 'Take the bull by the horns' means to deal with a difficult situation in a direct and confident way.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
The scandal that was uncovered turned out to be just the tip of the iceberg.
The idiom 'the tip of the iceberg' means:
options: the complete solution to a problem
a small, visible part of a much larger problem
questions.explanation: 'The tip of the iceberg' means only a small, noticeable part of a much bigger issue.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
The young entrepreneur decided to throw caution to the wind and invest all his savings.
The idiom 'throw caution to the wind' means:
options: to act recklessly without worrying about the consequences
to plan very carefully before acting
questions.explanation: 'Throw caution to the wind' means to take a risk without worrying about the danger involved.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
After his health scare, he decided to turn over a new leaf and start exercising.
The idiom 'turn over a new leaf' means:
options: to begin behaving in a better or different way
to move to a new location
questions.explanation: 'Turn over a new leaf' means to change one's behaviour for the better; to make a fresh start.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
The manager warned the staff to walk on eggshells around the strict new director.
The idiom 'walk on eggshells' means:
options: to behave very cautiously to avoid upsetting someone
questions.explanation: 'Walk on eggshells' means to be very careful about what you say or do so as not to upset someone.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
Unlike most people, she wears her heart on her sleeve and shows her emotions openly.
The idiom 'wear one's heart on one's sleeve' means:
options: to pretend to feel something one doesn't
questions.explanation: 'Wear your heart on your sleeve' means to show your emotions openly rather than hiding them.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
The committee decided to zero in on the main cause of the delay.
The idiom 'zero in on' means:
options: to focus attention closely on something specific
to reduce a budget to nothing
questions.explanation: 'Zero in on' means to direct all of one's attention toward a specific target or issue.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
Stop chatting and let's get down to business.
The idiom 'get down to business' means:
options: to start dealing with the main matter seriously
questions.explanation: 'Get down to business' means to begin discussing or working on the main task at hand.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
The comment about his old failure hit close to home.
The idiom 'hit close to home' means:
options: to miss the intended target completely
to affect someone personally because it relates to their own experience
questions.explanation: 'Hit close to home' means something affects a person deeply because it relates to their own life or experience.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
When she lost her job too, she realised they were in the same boat.
The idiom 'in the same boat' means:
options: in the same difficult situation as someone else
questions.explanation: 'In the same boat' means to be in the same difficult or unpleasant situation as someone else.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
The manager asked the staff to keep the merger under wraps for now.
The idiom 'keep something under wraps' means:
questions.explanation: 'Keep something under wraps' means to keep something secret or hidden from others.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
Getting upset over a tiny typo is making a mountain out of a molehill.
The idiom 'make a mountain out of a molehill' means:
options: to exaggerate a minor problem into a serious one
to solve a huge problem easily
questions.explanation: 'Make a mountain out of a molehill' means to treat a small problem as if it were much more serious.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
His name was on the tip of my tongue, but I just could not recall it.
The idiom 'on the tip of one's tongue' means:
options: almost remembered but not quite recalled
questions.explanation: 'On the tip of one's tongue' means something is almost remembered but cannot quite be recalled at that moment.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
Announcing the wedding date before booking the venue was putting the cart before the horse.
The idiom 'put the cart before the horse' means:
options: to do things in the wrong order
to travel using an old-fashioned method
questions.explanation: 'Put the cart before the horse' means to do things in the wrong order, reversing the natural or logical sequence.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
After the profit warnings, investors saw the writing on the wall for the company.
The idiom 'the writing on the wall' means:
options: a message painted on a building
clear signs that something bad is going to happen
questions.explanation: 'The writing on the wall' means clear signs that indicate a bad situation or failure is coming.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
Instead of admitting his own mistake, he threw his colleague under the bus.
The idiom 'throw someone under the bus' means:
options: to help someone cross the road safely
to blame or betray someone to protect oneself
questions.explanation: 'Throw someone under the bus' means to sacrifice or blame another person to save oneself from trouble.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
New staff are given a week of training to get up to speed with company procedures.
The idiom 'get up to speed' means:
options: to lose track of recent events
to become familiar with the current situation or information
questions.explanation: 'Get up to speed' means to acquire the most current information or become familiar with a situation.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
The missing file had been under his nose the entire time.
The idiom 'under one's nose' means:
options: in plain sight but not noticed
questions.explanation: 'Under one's nose' means something is in plain view yet not noticed.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
After the promotion, she finally felt she was in the driver's seat of her career.
The idiom 'in the driver's seat' means:
questions.explanation: 'In the driver's seat' means to be in control of a situation or in charge of decision-making.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
After months of financial strain, the small business was at the end of its rope.
The idiom 'at the end of one's rope' means:
options: having no more patience or resources left
questions.explanation: 'At the end of one's rope' means having no more strength, patience, or resources to continue coping with a situation.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
The younger boxer managed to beat his rival to the punch in the first round.
The idiom 'beat someone to the punch' means:
options: to act before someone else does
questions.explanation: 'Beat someone to the punch' means to do something before someone else gets the chance to do it.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
Rather than explaining every detail, the manager decided to cut to the chase.
The idiom 'cut to the chase' means:
options: to end a car chase safely
to get to the main point without wasting time
to avoid a difficult topic entirely
questions.explanation: 'Cut to the chase' means to get straight to the point without unnecessary details.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
After a few days on the job, the new intern began to get the hang of it.
The idiom 'get the hang of it' means:
options: to give up on a difficult job
to lose interest in a task
to learn how to do something properly
questions.explanation: 'Get the hang of it' means to begin to understand how to do something correctly through practice.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
With bills piling up and no income, the family was in a real pickle.
The idiom 'in a pickle' means:
options: in a happy and relaxed mood
in a difficult or awkward situation
questions.explanation: 'In a pickle' means to be in a difficult or troublesome situation.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
To get the contract approved, the manager had to jump through hoops.
The idiom 'jump through hoops' means:
options: to go through many difficult steps to achieve something
questions.explanation: 'Jump through hoops' means to go through a series of difficult or complicated steps to achieve a goal.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
He ignored the warnings and learned the hard way that honesty is important.
The idiom 'learn the hard way' means:
options: to learn something through difficult or unpleasant experience
to learn something quickly from a book
to be taught by an expert teacher
questions.explanation: 'Learn the hard way' means to learn something through personal difficulty or failure rather than being told.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Which of the underlined words is a noun? 'The BRAVERY of the soldier inspired the whole village.'
questions.explanation: 'Bravery' is an abstract noun naming a quality that cannot be touched or seen.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the proper noun in the sentence: 'Chidinma travelled to Lagos for the conference.'
questions.explanation: A proper noun names a specific person, place, or thing and is always capitalised, like 'Chidinma'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Which word in the sentence is a collective noun? 'The committee will announce its decision tomorrow.'
questions.explanation: A collective noun refers to a group treated as a single unit, such as 'committee', 'team', or 'flock'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Pick the abstract noun: 'Her honesty earned her the respect of everyone in the office.'
questions.explanation: 'Honesty' is an abstract noun because it names a quality, not something physical.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Which word functions as a common noun in this sentence? 'The teacher praised the student for his diligence.'
questions.explanation: 'Teacher' is a common noun — a general name for a person, not a specific one.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the noun used as the subject: 'Patience is a virtue every leader must possess.'
questions.explanation: 'Patience' is the subject noun of the sentence, the thing being discussed.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Which underlined word is a countable noun? 'She bought three CHAIRS for the new office.'
questions.explanation: 'Chairs' is countable because it can be counted (one chair, two chairs, three chairs).

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Which word is an uncountable noun in the sentence 'We need more information before deciding'?
questions.explanation: 'Information' is uncountable; we do not say 'one information' or 'two informations'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Which of the following is a compound noun? 'The mother-in-law arrived early for the ceremony.'
questions.explanation: A compound noun is made up of two or more words functioning as a single noun, like 'mother-in-law'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the possessive noun in the sentence: 'The student's essay impressed the examiner.'
questions.explanation: 'Student's' shows possession, indicating the essay belongs to the student.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Which word is a noun functioning as a direct object? 'The farmer planted maize before the rains came.'
questions.explanation: 'Maize' receives the action of the verb 'planted', making it the direct object.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Pick the noun that functions as an indirect object: 'She gave her brother a new book.'
questions.explanation: 'Brother' is the indirect object, receiving the direct object 'book' through the action 'gave'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Which word is a verbal noun (gerund) in the sentence 'Reading improves the mind'?
questions.explanation: 'Reading' is a gerund — a verb form ending in -ing used as a noun, here functioning as the subject.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the noun in apposition: 'Mr Adeyemi, our headmaster, addressed the students.'
questions.explanation: 'Our headmaster' renames 'Mr Adeyemi', giving more information about the same person; this is a noun in apposition.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Which word is a material noun in the sentence 'The bracelet was made of gold'?
questions.explanation: 'Gold' names a substance or material, making it a material noun.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Which word is a personal pronoun? 'She will attend the meeting on behalf of the manager.'
questions.explanation: 'She' is a personal pronoun referring to a specific person already known from context.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the possessive pronoun: 'This umbrella is mine, not yours.'
questions.explanation: 'Mine' is a possessive pronoun showing ownership without needing a noun after it.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Which pronoun in the sentence is reflexive? 'He blamed himself for the mistake.'
questions.explanation: 'Himself' is a reflexive pronoun referring back to the subject of the sentence, 'He'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Pick the relative pronoun: 'The man who called yesterday is my uncle.'
questions.explanation: 'Who' is a relative pronoun that introduces a clause describing 'the man'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Which word is a demonstrative pronoun? 'This is the best solution to the problem.'
questions.explanation: 'This' is a demonstrative pronoun pointing to a specific thing already mentioned or understood.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the interrogative pronoun: 'Who telephoned the office this morning?'
questions.explanation: 'Who' is an interrogative pronoun used to ask a question about a person.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Which pronoun is indefinite in this sentence? 'Everyone was pleased with the result of the match.'
questions.explanation: 'Everyone' is an indefinite pronoun; it does not refer to any specific, named person.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the reciprocal pronoun: 'The two friends helped each other with their assignments.'
questions.explanation: 'Each other' is a reciprocal pronoun showing a mutual action between two people.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Which word replaces the noun correctly as an object pronoun? 'The teacher called ___ to the front of the class.' (referring to the boy)
questions.explanation: 'Him' is the correct object pronoun to use after the verb 'called'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the pronoun functioning as the subject: 'They arrived before the ceremony began.'
questions.explanation: 'They' functions as the subject pronoun performing the action 'arrived'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct pronoun: 'Just between you and ___, I think he is wrong.'
questions.explanation: After a preposition like 'between', the object pronoun 'me' is required, not the subject pronoun 'I'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the emphatic pronoun in the sentence: 'The principal himself opened the new library.'
questions.explanation: 'Himself' is used here for emphasis, stressing that the principal personally performed the action; this is an emphatic (intensive) pronoun.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Which word is the main verb in the sentence 'The children played happily in the field'?
questions.explanation: 'Played' is the main verb, showing the action performed by the subject 'children'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the auxiliary verb: 'She has finished her assignment already.'
questions.explanation: 'Has' is an auxiliary (helping) verb that works with 'finished' to form the present perfect tense.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Which sentence contains a transitive verb? Choose the sentence where the verb takes a direct object.
questions.explanation: 'Kicked' is transitive because it acts on a direct object, 'the ball'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Which sentence contains an intransitive verb (no direct object)?
questions.explanation: 'Barked' does not require a direct object to complete its meaning; it is intransitive.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the modal verb in the sentence: 'You must submit your project before Friday.'
questions.explanation: 'Must' is a modal verb expressing obligation or necessity.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Which word is a linking verb in the sentence 'The soup tastes delicious'?
questions.explanation: 'Tastes' links the subject 'soup' to the adjective 'delicious' describing it, making it a linking verb.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct past tense form of the irregular verb 'to swim'.
questions.explanation: The simple past tense of 'swim' is 'swam'; 'swum' is the past participle used with an auxiliary verb.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Which verb form correctly completes the sentence? 'By next year, she ___ from university.'
questions.explanation: The future perfect tense 'will have graduated' shows an action that will be completed before a future point in time.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the gerund (verb acting as a noun) in the sentence: 'Swimming is her favourite hobby.'
questions.explanation: 'Swimming' functions as a noun here (a gerund), acting as the subject of the sentence.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Which word is used as an infinitive in the sentence 'She wants to travel abroad next year'?
questions.explanation: 'To travel' is an infinitive — the base form of the verb preceded by 'to' — functioning as the object of 'wants'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct verb form: 'She suggested that he ___ the report before the meeting.'
questions.explanation: After verbs like 'suggest' expressing a recommendation, the subjunctive base form 'revise' is used, regardless of the subject.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the causative verb structure: 'The manager had the documents delivered before noon.'
questions.explanation: 'Had...delivered' is a causative structure showing the subject arranged for someone else to perform the action.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Which verb form correctly completes the sentence? 'I would rather you ___ that decision alone.'
questions.explanation: After 'would rather' referring to someone else's action, the past subjunctive form 'made' is used even though the meaning is present or future.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the adjective in the sentence: 'The tall building collapsed during the storm.'
questions.explanation: 'Tall' describes the noun 'building', making it an adjective.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Which word is a demonstrative adjective? 'These shoes belong to my sister.'
questions.explanation: 'These' modifies the noun 'shoes' and points out which ones, making it a demonstrative adjective.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the comparative form of the adjective 'good'.
questions.explanation: 'Better' is the correct comparative form of the irregular adjective 'good'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the superlative form of the adjective 'bad'.
questions.explanation: 'Worst' is the correct superlative form of the irregular adjective 'bad'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the possessive adjective: 'Our school won the debate competition this year.'
questions.explanation: 'Our' modifies the noun 'school' and shows possession, making it a possessive adjective.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Which word functions as a quantitative adjective in the sentence 'Several students missed the test'?
questions.explanation: 'Several' modifies 'students' by indicating an indefinite quantity, making it a quantitative adjective.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the adjective formed from a verb (participial adjective): 'The broken chair was thrown away.'
questions.explanation: 'Broken' is a past participle used as an adjective describing the noun 'chair'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Which sentence uses the adjective correctly in its comparative form?
options: This road is longer than that one.
This road is more longer than that one.
This road is longest than that one.
This road is long than that one.
questions.explanation: The comparative of the one-syllable adjective 'long' is formed by adding '-er': 'longer'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the predicative adjective in the sentence: 'The weather became very cold overnight.'
questions.explanation: 'Cold' comes after the linking verb 'became' and describes the subject 'weather', making it predicative.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct order of adjectives: 'She bought a ___ table.'
questions.explanation: Standard English adjective order is size, shape, then material: small (size), round (shape), wooden (material).

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the adjective functioning as a complement: 'The results made the students happy.'
questions.explanation: 'Happy' completes the meaning of the object 'students' after the verb 'made', functioning as an object complement.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct interrogative adjective: '___ book is this on the table?'
questions.explanation: 'Whose' functions as an interrogative adjective modifying the noun 'book' to ask about ownership.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the adverb of manner in the sentence: 'She sang beautifully at the concert.'
questions.explanation: 'Beautifully' describes how the action 'sang' was performed, making it an adverb of manner.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Which word is an adverb of time? 'They will arrive tomorrow morning.'
questions.explanation: 'Tomorrow' tells us when the action will happen, making it an adverb of time.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the adverb of place in the sentence: 'Please put the books there.'
questions.explanation: 'There' indicates the location where the action should happen, making it an adverb of place.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Which word is an adverb of frequency? 'He always arrives early for work.'
questions.explanation: 'Always' tells us how often the action happens, making it an adverb of frequency.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the adverb of degree in the sentence: 'The exam was extremely difficult this term.'
questions.explanation: 'Extremely' intensifies the adjective 'difficult', making it an adverb of degree.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct adverb form of the adjective 'careful'.
questions.explanation: The adverb form of 'careful' is made by adding '-ly': 'carefully'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Which word functions as an interrogative adverb in the sentence 'Why did you leave the meeting early?'
questions.explanation: 'Why' is an interrogative adverb used to ask about the reason for an action.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the adverb that modifies another adverb: 'She finished the race very quickly.'
questions.explanation: 'Very' modifies the adverb 'quickly', intensifying it.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Which sentence uses an adverb correctly to modify an adjective?
questions.explanation: 'Really' is an adverb correctly modifying the adjective 'delicious'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the conjunctive adverb in the sentence: 'She was tired; nevertheless, she finished the race.'
questions.explanation: 'Nevertheless' connects two independent clauses while showing contrast, making it a conjunctive adverb.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the relative adverb in the sentence: 'This is the village where I was born.'
questions.explanation: 'Where' introduces a clause modifying 'village' and refers to a place, making it a relative adverb.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct adverb to complete the sentence: 'She did ___ in the examination than expected.'
questions.explanation: 'Better' is the comparative form of the adverb 'well', correctly used here to compare performance.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the adverb of certainty in the sentence: 'She will definitely attend the ceremony.'
questions.explanation: 'Definitely' expresses the speaker's certainty about the action, making it an adverb of certainty.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct preposition: 'The keys are ___ the drawer.'
questions.explanation: 'In' is used to show something is enclosed within a space, like a drawer.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct preposition: 'We will meet ___ Monday morning.'
questions.explanation: 'On' is used with specific days, such as 'on Monday'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct preposition: 'The plane flew ___ the clouds.'
questions.explanation: 'Above' indicates a position higher than the clouds without touching them.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct preposition: 'She has been ill ___ Tuesday.'
questions.explanation: 'Since' is used with a specific point in time when the action began.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct preposition: 'He apologised ___ arriving late.'
questions.explanation: 'Apologise for' is the correct collocation used before a noun or gerund.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct preposition: 'The children are afraid ___ the dark.'
questions.explanation: 'Afraid of' is the standard collocation used to express fear of something.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct preposition: 'She is married ___ a doctor.'
questions.explanation: 'Married to' is the correct fixed preposition used with a spouse's profession or identity.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct preposition: 'The book was written ___ a famous author.'
questions.explanation: 'By' introduces the agent responsible for an action, especially in passive constructions.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct preposition: 'They travelled ___ car to the village.'
questions.explanation: 'By' is used before a means of transport without an article, as in 'by car', 'by bus'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct preposition: 'The decision depends ___ the outcome of the vote.'
questions.explanation: 'Depend on' is the fixed collocation used before the thing something relies on.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct preposition: 'The committee is looking ___ ways to reduce costs.'
questions.explanation: 'Looking for' is the correct collocation meaning to search for or seek something.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct preposition: 'She is good ___ solving mathematical problems.'
questions.explanation: 'Good at' is the standard collocation used to describe a skill or ability.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the coordinating conjunction: 'She wanted to travel, but she had no money.'
questions.explanation: 'But' joins two independent clauses of contrasting meaning, making it a coordinating conjunction.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Which word is a subordinating conjunction? 'Although it rained, the match continued.'
questions.explanation: 'Although' introduces a subordinate clause showing contrast, making it a subordinating conjunction.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the correlative conjunction pair used correctly: 'She is ___ intelligent ___ hardworking.'
questions.explanation: 'Both...and' is a correlative conjunction pair used to join two equally emphasised items.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct conjunction: 'You must study hard ___ you will fail the exam.'
questions.explanation: 'Or' expresses an alternative or consequence if the first condition is not met.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the conjunction used to show a reason: 'He stayed home because he was unwell.'
questions.explanation: 'Because' introduces a clause that gives the reason for the main clause.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct conjunction: '___ she was tired, she finished her homework.'
questions.explanation: 'Even though' shows a contrast between being tired and still finishing the homework, similar to 'although'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the conjunction that shows purpose: 'She studied hard so that she could pass the exam.'
questions.explanation: 'So that' introduces a clause of purpose, explaining why the action was taken.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct correlative conjunction: 'He is ___ a teacher ___ a farmer.'
questions.explanation: 'Neither...nor' correctly pairs to express that both possibilities are false.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the conjunction expressing condition: 'Unless you apologise, she will not forgive you.'
questions.explanation: 'Unless' introduces a condition meaning 'if not'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the conjunction that best completes the sentence: 'He was exhausted, ___ he kept working.'
questions.explanation: 'Yet' shows an unexpected contrast between being exhausted and continuing to work.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct correlative conjunction: 'She was ___ talented ___ hardworking.'
questions.explanation: 'Not only...but also' is the correct correlative conjunction pair used to add emphasis to two related qualities.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the conjunction that shows an unexpected result: 'He studied hard; however, he failed the exam.'
questions.explanation: 'However' is a conjunctive adverb showing contrast between the expected and actual result.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the interjection in the sentence: 'Wow! That was an amazing performance.'
questions.explanation: 'Wow' is an interjection expressing sudden surprise or admiration.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Which word is an interjection expressing pain? 'Ouch! I just stepped on a nail.'
questions.explanation: 'Ouch' is an interjection used to express sudden pain.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the interjection: 'Alas, the old bridge finally collapsed.'
questions.explanation: 'Alas' is an interjection expressing sorrow or regret.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Which word functions as an interjection of joy? 'Hurray! We won the championship.'
questions.explanation: 'Hurray' is an interjection expressing joy or triumph.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the interjection used to call for attention: 'Hey! Watch where you are going.'
questions.explanation: 'Hey' is an interjection used to attract someone's attention.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Which word is an interjection expressing disgust? 'Ugh! This food tastes terrible.'
questions.explanation: 'Ugh' is an interjection expressing disgust or displeasure.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the interjection expressing relief: 'Phew! We made it just in time.'
questions.explanation: 'Phew' is an interjection expressing relief after a stressful moment.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Which word functions as an interjection of hesitation? 'Well, I am not sure that is correct.'
questions.explanation: 'Well' can function as an interjection expressing hesitation or thoughtful pause.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the interjection expressing agreement: 'Indeed! That is exactly what happened.'
questions.explanation: 'Indeed' functions as an interjection here, emphatically confirming agreement.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Which word is an interjection expressing warning? 'Beware! The road ahead is dangerous.'
questions.explanation: 'Beware' functions as an interjection warning of danger.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the interjection expressing sudden realisation: 'Oh! I forgot to bring my textbook.'
questions.explanation: 'Oh' is an interjection expressing sudden realisation or surprise.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct tense: 'By the time the fire service arrived, the building ___ already collapsed.'
questions.explanation: The past perfect 'had collapsed' shows an action completed before another past action (the arrival).

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct tense: 'No sooner ___ he arrived than the meeting started.'
questions.explanation: 'No sooner had he arrived' uses the past perfect after the inverted structure 'no sooner...than'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct tense: 'The road ___ still not finished after three years of construction.'
questions.explanation: The present perfect continuous idea is expressed here with 'has been', showing an ongoing unfinished state.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct tense: 'She ___ in Lagos since 2015.'
questions.explanation: The present perfect 'has lived' is used with 'since' to show an action continuing from the past to the present.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct tense: 'When I got home, my mother ___ dinner already.'
questions.explanation: The past perfect 'had cooked' shows an action completed before another past action (getting home).

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct tense: 'They ___ football every Saturday when they were in secondary school.'
questions.explanation: The simple past 'played' describes a repeated habitual action in the past.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct tense: 'While she ___ dinner, the phone rang.'
questions.explanation: The past continuous 'was cooking' shows an ongoing action interrupted by another past event.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct tense: 'By next December, she ___ her degree.'
questions.explanation: The future perfect 'will have completed' shows an action that will be finished before a specific point in the future.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct tense: 'I ___ him since we graduated from university.'
questions.explanation: The present perfect negative 'have not seen' is used with 'since' to show an action that has not happened up to now.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct tense: 'The train ___ before we reached the station.'
questions.explanation: The past perfect 'had left' shows the train's departure happened before another past action (reaching the station).

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct tense: 'She usually ___ to work by bus, but today she is driving.'
questions.explanation: The simple present 'goes' expresses a habitual action.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct tense: 'If it rains tomorrow, we ___ the picnic.'
questions.explanation: The first conditional uses the simple future 'will cancel' in the main clause with a present tense in the if-clause.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct tense: 'If I had studied harder, I ___ the examination.'
questions.explanation: The third conditional uses 'would have passed' to describe an unreal past result.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct tense: 'He ___ for the company for ten years before he retired.'
questions.explanation: The past perfect 'had worked' shows the duration of an action completed before another past event (retirement).

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct tense: 'Look! The children ___ in the rain.'
questions.explanation: The present continuous 'are playing' describes an action happening right now.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct tense: 'She ___ her homework by the time her mother returned.'
questions.explanation: The past perfect 'had finished' shows the homework was completed before the mother's return.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct tense: 'They ___ to Ghana twice this year.'
questions.explanation: The present perfect 'have travelled' is used for repeated actions within a period that is not yet finished (this year).

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct tense: 'By the time you arrive, I ___ the presentation.'
questions.explanation: The future perfect 'will have finished' shows an action completed before another future action.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct tense: 'She was surprised because she ___ him in years.'
questions.explanation: The past perfect negative 'had not seen' shows a state that had persisted up to a point in the past.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct tense: 'Water ___ at one hundred degrees Celsius at sea level.'
questions.explanation: The simple present 'boils' is used to state a scientific fact or general truth.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct tense: 'She ___ television when the power went off.'
questions.explanation: The past continuous 'was watching' shows an ongoing action that was interrupted by another past event.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct tense: 'I wish I ___ more time to prepare for the exam.'
questions.explanation: After 'I wish' expressing a present unreal wish, the past subjunctive 'had' is used.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct tense: 'If she ___ harder, she would have passed the test.'
questions.explanation: The third conditional requires the past perfect 'had studied' in the if-clause to describe an unreal past condition.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct tense: 'The company ___ its policies since the new manager took over.'
questions.explanation: The present perfect 'has changed' links a past action to its relevance in the present.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct tense: 'They ___ dinner by the time we arrived at the party.'
questions.explanation: The past perfect 'had finished' shows an action completed before another past event (our arrival).

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct tense: 'She ___ abroad next semester as part of an exchange programme.'
questions.explanation: The present continuous can express a planned future arrangement, as in 'is studying' for next semester.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct tense: 'I ___ this book twice already.'
questions.explanation: The present perfect 'have read' is used to show a completed action with present relevance, especially with 'already'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct tense: 'By the time she turns eighteen, she ___ to five different countries.'
questions.explanation: The future perfect 'will have travelled' shows an action expected to be completed before a specific future point (her eighteenth birthday).

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct tense: 'He always ___ his hands before eating.'
questions.explanation: The simple present 'washes' describes a regular habitual action.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct tense: 'The workers ___ the road for six months when the funds ran out.'
questions.explanation: The past perfect continuous 'had been repairing' emphasises the duration of an action leading up to another past event.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct verb: 'Neither the principal nor the teachers ___ informed about the change.'
questions.explanation: With 'neither...nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject, which here is the plural 'teachers'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct verb: 'The number of applicants ___ increased significantly this year.'
questions.explanation: 'The number of' takes a singular verb because 'number' itself is the subject, not the applicants.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct verb: 'A number of students ___ absent from school today.'
questions.explanation: 'A number of' takes a plural verb because it refers to several individual students.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct verb: 'Bread and butter ___ his favourite breakfast.'
questions.explanation: 'Bread and butter' is treated as a single idea (a compound subject referring to one dish), so it takes a singular verb.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct verb: 'Each of the students ___ required to submit an assignment.'
questions.explanation: 'Each' is always singular, regardless of the plural noun that follows it.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct verb: 'Either the manager or his assistants ___ responsible for the error.'
questions.explanation: With 'either...or', the verb agrees with the nearer subject, which here is the plural 'assistants'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct verb: 'The jury ___ divided over the verdict.'
questions.explanation: 'Jury' is a collective noun that takes a singular verb when acting as a single unit.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct verb: 'None of the information ___ useful for the report.'
questions.explanation: 'None of' with an uncountable noun like 'information' takes a singular verb.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct verb: 'The news about the accident ___ shocking.'
questions.explanation: 'News' is always treated as singular in English, despite ending in 's'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct verb: 'Mathematics ___ my favourite subject in school.'
questions.explanation: Subjects like 'Mathematics', 'Physics', and 'Economics' are treated as singular despite ending in 's'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct verb: 'The scissors ___ on the table.'
questions.explanation: Tools that come in two parts, like 'scissors' and 'trousers', are treated as plural.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct verb: 'Ten kilometres ___ a long distance to walk every day.'
questions.explanation: A measurement expressed as a single quantity, like 'ten kilometres', takes a singular verb.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct verb: 'One of the reasons for his success ___ hard work.'
questions.explanation: The subject is 'one', which is singular, so the verb must also be singular.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct verb: 'The police ___ investigating the robbery.'
questions.explanation: 'Police' is always treated as a plural noun in English.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct verb: 'My family ___ planning a trip to the village next month.'
questions.explanation: 'Family' is a collective noun treated as singular when referring to the unit acting together.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct verb: 'Either of the answers ___ acceptable.'
questions.explanation: 'Either' used alone (without 'or') is singular.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct verb: 'The committee members ___ yet to reach an agreement.'
questions.explanation: When 'committee' is followed by 'members', the plural noun takes precedence and the verb becomes plural.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct verb: 'Everybody in the class ___ present today.'
questions.explanation: Indefinite pronouns like 'everybody', 'everyone', and 'somebody' are always singular.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct verb: 'The majority of the students ___ in favour of the new rule.'
questions.explanation: 'The majority of' agrees with the plural noun that follows it, here 'students'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct verb: 'Physics and chemistry ___ compulsory subjects for science students.'
questions.explanation: When two distinct subjects are joined by 'and' as separate items, the verb is plural.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct verb: 'The rice and beans ___ ready to be served.'
questions.explanation: 'Rice and beans' is treated as one combined dish here, so it takes a singular verb.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct verb: 'Not only the students but also the teacher ___ excited about the trip.'
questions.explanation: With 'not only...but also', the verb agrees with the nearer subject, which here is the singular 'teacher'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct verb: 'Ten years ___ a long time to wait for justice.'
questions.explanation: A period of time treated as a single unit, such as 'ten years', takes a singular verb.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct verb: 'Economics ___ taught as a compulsory subject in this school.'
questions.explanation: 'Economics' is a subject name ending in 's' that is treated as singular.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct verb: 'Every one of the applicants ___ interviewed yesterday.'
questions.explanation: 'Every one of' takes a singular verb because 'every' makes the subject singular, regardless of the plural noun following it.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct verb: 'A pair of shoes ___ missing from the shelf.'
questions.explanation: 'A pair of' is treated as a singular unit, so the verb agrees in the singular.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct verb: 'The team ___ celebrating their individual achievements separately.'
questions.explanation: When a collective noun like 'team' refers to its members acting as individuals rather than a unit, the verb can be plural.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct verb: 'Fifty naira ___ not enough to buy bread these days.'
questions.explanation: A sum of money treated as a single amount, like 'fifty naira', takes a singular verb.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct verb: 'One-third of the workers ___ absent due to the strike.'
questions.explanation: Fractions agree with the noun that follows 'of', here the plural 'workers', so the verb is plural.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct verb: 'The government, along with several ministries, ___ reviewing the budget.'
questions.explanation: Phrases introduced by 'along with', 'together with', or 'as well as' do not affect the number of the main subject, which remains singular here ('the government').

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the noun clause in the sentence: 'What she said surprised everyone in the room.'
questions.explanation: 'What she said' functions as the subject of the sentence, making it a noun clause.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: What grammatical function does the underlined clause perform? 'I believe THAT HE IS INNOCENT.'
questions.explanation: The noun clause 'that he is innocent' functions as the direct object of the verb 'believe'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the noun clause: 'The teacher explained why the experiment had failed.'
questions.explanation: 'Why the experiment had failed' acts as the object of the verb 'explained', making it a noun clause.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: What function does the noun clause perform? 'WHOEVER WINS THE RACE will receive a trophy.'
questions.explanation: 'Whoever wins the race' functions as the subject of the sentence.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the noun clause functioning as a complement: 'The truth is that he never attended the meeting.'
options: that he never attended the meeting
questions.explanation: The clause 'that he never attended the meeting' completes the meaning of the subject 'the truth', making it a subject complement.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Which part of the sentence is a noun clause? 'Nobody knows what caused the sudden blackout.'
questions.explanation: 'What caused the sudden blackout' functions as the object of the verb 'knows', making it a noun clause.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the function of the underlined clause: 'She asked WHETHER THE FLIGHT HAD BEEN DELAYED.'
questions.explanation: The noun clause 'whether the flight had been delayed' is the direct object of the verb 'asked'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the noun clause: 'That the government would raise taxes was widely expected.'
options: That the government would raise taxes
questions.explanation: This noun clause functions as the subject of the sentence.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Which clause functions as the object of the preposition in the sentence 'I am interested in whatever you have to say'?
questions.explanation: 'Whatever you have to say' is a noun clause functioning as the object of the preposition 'in'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the noun clause: 'He wondered if the letter had reached her in time.'
options: if the letter had reached her in time
questions.explanation: 'If the letter had reached her in time' functions as the object of the verb 'wondered', making it a noun clause.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the noun clause functioning as the object of a preposition: 'Give the prize to whoever finishes first.'
questions.explanation: 'Whoever finishes first' functions as the object of the preposition 'to', making it a noun clause.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the noun clause: 'What the manager decided will affect everyone in the office.'
questions.explanation: 'What the manager decided' functions as the subject of the sentence, making it a noun clause.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Which clause functions as the object in the sentence 'I do not know when the flight will arrive'?
questions.explanation: 'When the flight will arrive' functions as the object of the verb 'know', making it a noun clause.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the noun clause acting as a subject complement: 'My only wish is that everyone stays safe.'
questions.explanation: 'That everyone stays safe' completes the meaning of the subject 'my only wish', functioning as a subject complement.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Which clause functions as a noun clause in the sentence 'How she solved the puzzle amazed her classmates'?
questions.explanation: 'How she solved the puzzle' functions as the subject of the sentence, making it a noun clause.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the noun clause: 'The officer confirmed that the road had been repaired.'
options: that the road had been repaired
questions.explanation: 'That the road had been repaired' functions as the object of the verb 'confirmed', making it a noun clause.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Which clause functions as a noun clause in 'She could not decide which dress to wear'?
questions.explanation: 'Which dress to wear' functions as the object of the verb 'decide', making it a noun clause.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the noun clause: 'It is surprising that he passed the test without studying.'
options: that he passed the test without studying
questions.explanation: 'That he passed the test without studying' is the real subject of the sentence, with 'it' as a placeholder subject.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Which clause is a noun clause in 'I am not certain whether she received my message'?
questions.explanation: 'Whether she received my message' functions as the object of the adjective phrase 'am not certain', making it a noun clause.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the noun clause: 'Whoever arrives late will not be allowed into the hall.'
questions.explanation: 'Whoever arrives late' functions as the subject of the sentence, making it a noun clause.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the adjectival clause in the sentence: 'The man who called yesterday is my uncle.'
questions.explanation: 'Who called yesterday' describes the noun 'man', making it an adjectival (relative) clause.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: What does the adjectival clause modify in the sentence 'The book that I borrowed was very interesting'?
questions.explanation: 'That I borrowed' is an adjectival clause modifying the noun 'book'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the adjectival clause: 'The house where I grew up has been demolished.'
questions.explanation: 'Where I grew up' describes the noun 'house', making it an adjectival clause introduced by a relative adverb.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Which clause functions adjectivally in the sentence 'Students whose grades improve will receive a prize'?
questions.explanation: 'Whose grades improve' modifies 'students', making it an adjectival clause.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the adjectival clause: 'The reason why she resigned remains unclear.'
questions.explanation: 'Why she resigned' modifies the noun 'reason', making it an adjectival clause.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Which clause describes the noun 'car' in the sentence 'The car that was stolen has been recovered'?
questions.explanation: 'That was stolen' is an adjectival clause describing the noun 'car'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the non-defining adjectival clause: 'My brother, who lives in Kano, is visiting us this weekend.'
questions.explanation: 'Who lives in Kano' adds extra, non-essential information about 'my brother', making it a non-defining adjectival clause.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Which word correctly introduces the adjectival clause in 'The professor whom we invited could not attend'?
questions.explanation: 'Whom' is the correct relative pronoun as the object of the verb 'invited' referring to a person.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the adjectival clause modifying 'time' in the sentence 'There was a time when things were simpler.'
questions.explanation: 'When things were simpler' modifies the noun 'time', making it an adjectival clause.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Which clause functions adjectivally in 'The company that hired her went bankrupt last year'?
questions.explanation: 'That hired her' describes the noun 'company', making it an adjectival clause.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the adjectival clause: 'Anyone who breaks the rule will be punished.'
questions.explanation: 'Who breaks the rule' modifies 'anyone', making it an adjectival clause.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Which clause modifies 'gift' in the sentence 'The gift that she gave me was very thoughtful'?
questions.explanation: 'That she gave me' describes the noun 'gift', making it an adjectival clause.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the adjectival clause: 'The village in which she was born no longer exists.'
questions.explanation: 'In which she was born' modifies the noun 'village', making it an adjectival clause.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Which clause functions adjectivally in 'The teacher, whose patience is legendary, calmed the class'?
questions.explanation: 'Whose patience is legendary' adds descriptive information about 'the teacher', making it an adjectival clause.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the adjectival clause: 'This is the school that produced many great scholars.'
questions.explanation: 'That produced many great scholars' describes the noun 'school', making it an adjectival clause.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Which clause modifies 'day' in the sentence 'I will never forget the day when we first met'?
questions.explanation: 'When we first met' modifies the noun 'day', making it an adjectival clause.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the adjectival clause: 'The candidate whom the panel selected impressed everyone.'
questions.explanation: 'Whom the panel selected' describes 'the candidate', making it an adjectival clause.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Which clause functions adjectivally in 'The reason that he gave was not convincing'?
questions.explanation: 'That he gave' modifies the noun 'reason', making it an adjectival clause.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the adjectival clause: 'People who exercise regularly tend to live longer.'
questions.explanation: 'Who exercise regularly' modifies the noun 'people', making it an adjectival clause.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Which clause modifies 'city' in the sentence 'Lagos, which is the commercial capital, attracts many investors'?
questions.explanation: 'Which is the commercial capital' adds extra information about 'Lagos', making it a non-defining adjectival clause.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the adverbial clause of time: 'She left the party before the fireworks began.'
questions.explanation: 'Before the fireworks began' tells us when the action happened, making it an adverbial clause of time.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the adverbial clause of reason: 'He failed the test because he did not study.'
questions.explanation: 'Because he did not study' gives the reason for the main clause, making it an adverbial clause of reason.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the adverbial clause of condition: 'If it rains tomorrow, the match will be postponed.'
questions.explanation: 'If it rains tomorrow' introduces a condition on which the main clause depends, making it an adverbial clause of condition.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the adverbial clause of concession: 'Although he was tired, he finished the race.'
questions.explanation: 'Although he was tired' shows a contrast with the main clause, making it an adverbial clause of concession.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the adverbial clause of place: 'They built the school where the old market used to stand.'
options: where the old market used to stand
questions.explanation: 'Where the old market used to stand' tells us the location of the action, making it an adverbial clause of place.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the adverbial clause of purpose: 'She saved money so that she could travel abroad.'
options: so that she could travel abroad
questions.explanation: 'So that she could travel abroad' explains the purpose of the main clause, making it an adverbial clause of purpose.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the adverbial clause of manner: 'He answered the question as if he had studied all night.'
options: as if he had studied all night
questions.explanation: 'As if he had studied all night' describes the manner in which he answered, making it an adverbial clause of manner.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the adverbial clause of result: 'She was so exhausted that she fell asleep immediately.'
questions.explanation: 'That she fell asleep immediately' shows the result of being exhausted, making it an adverbial clause of result.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the adverbial clause of comparison: 'She runs faster than her brother does.'
questions.explanation: 'Than her brother does' compares the subject's speed to another's, making it an adverbial clause of comparison.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the adverbial clause of time: 'As soon as the bell rang, the students rushed out.'
options: As soon as the bell rang
questions.explanation: 'As soon as the bell rang' tells us when the main action happened, making it an adverbial clause of time.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the adverbial clause of condition: 'Unless you leave now, you will miss the bus.'
questions.explanation: 'Unless you leave now' introduces a negative condition, making it an adverbial clause of condition.

questions.subject: English Language
