questions.text: Identify the adverbial clause of time: 'Since she moved to Lagos, she has visited home only twice.'
questions.explanation: 'Since she moved to Lagos' tells us the starting point of the action, making it an adverbial clause of time.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the adverbial clause of concession: 'Even though she apologised, he remained angry.'
questions.explanation: 'Even though she apologised' shows a contrast with the main clause, making it an adverbial clause of concession.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the adverbial clause of reason: 'Since the roads were flooded, the buses could not move.'
questions.explanation: 'Since the roads were flooded' gives the reason for the main clause, making it an adverbial clause of reason.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the adverbial clause of place: 'You may sit wherever you find a comfortable seat.'
options: wherever you find a comfortable seat
questions.explanation: 'Wherever you find a comfortable seat' tells us the location, making it an adverbial clause of place.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the adverbial clause of time: 'Until the results are announced, no one will know the winner.'
options: no one will know the winner
questions.explanation: 'Until the results are announced' tells us when the main clause's condition will change, making it an adverbial clause of time.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the adverbial clause of purpose: 'He whispered so as not to wake the baby.'
options: so as not to wake the baby
questions.explanation: 'So as not to wake the baby' explains the purpose behind the whispering, making it an adverbial clause of purpose.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the adverbial clause of condition: 'Provided that you complete the form, your application will be considered.'
options: Provided that you complete the form
questions.explanation: 'Provided that you complete the form' sets a condition for the main clause, making it an adverbial clause of condition.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the adverbial clause of manner: 'She organised the files as her supervisor had instructed.'
questions.explanation: 'As her supervisor had instructed' describes how the action was carried out, making it an adverbial clause of manner.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the adverbial clause of concession: 'Whatever happens, the team must remain united.'
questions.explanation: 'Whatever happens' concedes any possible outcome before stating the main point, making it an adverbial clause of concession.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Change to passive voice: 'The chef cooked the meal.'
options: The chef is cooking the meal.
The meal was cooked by the chef.
The meal has cooked the chef.
questions.explanation: In the passive voice, the object 'the meal' becomes the subject, and 'was cooked' shows the past passive form.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Change to passive voice: 'The workers are building a new bridge.'
options: A new bridge was building the workers.
The workers built a new bridge.
A new bridge builds the workers.
A new bridge is being built by the workers.
questions.explanation: The present continuous passive uses 'is being built' to match the tense of the active sentence.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Change to passive voice: 'They will announce the results tomorrow.'
options: The results will be announced tomorrow.
questions.explanation: The future passive is formed with 'will be' plus the past participle 'announced'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Change to passive voice: 'Someone has stolen my bicycle.'
questions.explanation: The present perfect passive is formed with 'has been' plus the past participle 'stolen'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Change to active voice: 'The letter was written by the secretary.'
options: The secretary has written the letter.
The secretary was writing the letter.
questions.explanation: In the active voice, the agent 'the secretary' becomes the subject performing the action.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Change to passive voice: 'The teacher will explain the topic tomorrow.'
options: The topic explains the teacher tomorrow.
The topic was explained by the teacher.
The topic will be explained by the teacher tomorrow.
questions.explanation: The future passive uses 'will be explained' to correspond with the active future tense.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Change to passive voice: 'People speak English all over the world.'
options: English is spoken all over the world.
English was spoken all over the world.
English speaks all over the world.
English has spoken all over the world.
questions.explanation: The present simple passive 'is spoken' is used for general, ongoing facts.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Change to active voice: 'The award was presented to her by the governor.'
options: The governor presented the award to her.
The governor was presenting to her.
She presented the award to the governor.
questions.explanation: The agent 'the governor' becomes the subject when converting to the active voice.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Change to passive voice: 'The company is reviewing the contract.'
options: The contract was reviewed the company.
The contract is being reviewed by the company.
questions.explanation: The present continuous passive is formed with 'is being reviewed'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Change to passive voice: 'They had completed the project before the deadline.'
options: The project was completing before the deadline.
The project completed before the deadline.
The project had been completed before the deadline.
The project has completed before the deadline.
questions.explanation: The past perfect passive is formed with 'had been' plus the past participle 'completed'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Which sentence is correctly written in the passive voice?
options: My sister was baking cake by.
The cake bakes by my sister.
The cake was baked by my sister.
questions.explanation: This sentence correctly places the object 'the cake' as the subject with the passive verb 'was baked'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Change to active voice: 'The window had been broken by the strong wind.'
options: The window has broken the wind.
The strong wind was broken by the window.
The window broke the strong wind.
The strong wind had broken the window.
questions.explanation: The agent 'the strong wind' becomes the subject in the active version.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Change to passive voice: 'The manager praised the staff for their hard work.'
options: The staff was praising the manager.
The manager was praised by the staff.
The staff were praised by the manager for their hard work.
questions.explanation: 'The staff' becomes the plural subject with the passive verb 'were praised'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Change to passive voice: 'The government has introduced a new policy.'
options: A new policy has been introduced by the government.
A new policy introduces the government.
questions.explanation: The present perfect passive 'has been introduced' matches the active present perfect tense.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Which sentence correctly uses the passive voice with a modal verb?
options: The report must submitted by Friday.
The report must submit by Friday.
The report must be submit by Friday.
The report must be submitted by Friday.
questions.explanation: The passive with a modal verb is formed as 'modal + be + past participle': 'must be submitted'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Change to active voice: 'A new law was passed by the legislature last week.'
options: A new law has passed the legislature.
A new law passed the legislature last week.
The legislature passed a new law last week.
The legislature was passing a new law.
questions.explanation: The agent 'the legislature' becomes the subject of the active sentence.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Change to passive voice: 'The judges will announce the winner at noon.'
options: The winner was announced by judges.
The winner will be announced by the judges at noon.
The winner will announce the judges at noon.
questions.explanation: The future passive 'will be announced' correctly matches the active future tense.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Change to passive voice: 'The fire destroyed several houses in the village.'
options: The fire was destroyed by several houses.
Several houses have destroyed the fire.
Several houses in the village were destroyed by the fire.
questions.explanation: 'Several houses' becomes the subject with the passive verb 'were destroyed'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Change to active voice: 'The children were being taught by a new teacher.'
options: The children have taught a new teacher.
The children taught a new teacher.
A new teacher taught by the children.
A new teacher was teaching the children.
questions.explanation: The agent 'a new teacher' becomes the subject in the active past continuous form.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Change to passive voice: 'The council will build a new market next year.'
options: A new market builds the council next year.
A new market was built by the council.
A new market has been built.
A new market will be built by the council next year.
questions.explanation: The future passive 'will be built' correctly reflects the tense of the original active sentence.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Change to active voice: 'The suspect was arrested by the police last night.'
options: The police was arresting the suspect.
The police arrested the suspect last night.
The suspect has arrested the police.
questions.explanation: The agent 'the police' becomes the subject in the active version.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Change to passive voice: 'The students must complete the assignment by Monday.'
options: The assignment must complete by Monday.
The assignment must be completed by Monday.
The assignment must completed by Monday.
The assignment is must completed by Monday.
questions.explanation: The modal passive is formed as 'modal + be + past participle': 'must be completed'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Change to passive voice: 'The librarian had arranged all the books before the visitors arrived.'
options: All the books had been arranged by the librarian before the visitors arrived.
All the books have arranged by the librarian.
All the books arranged the librarian.
All the books were arranging by the librarian.
questions.explanation: The past perfect passive is formed with 'had been' plus the past participle 'arranged'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Change to active voice: 'The proposal is being reviewed by the board of directors.'
options: The proposal has reviewed the board.
The board of directors was reviewed by the proposal.
The board of directors is reviewing the proposal.
questions.explanation: The agent 'the board of directors' becomes the subject in the active present continuous form.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Change to passive voice: 'The organizers will have completed the arrangements by Friday.'
options: The arrangements will complete by Friday.
The arrangements will have been completed by Friday.
The arrangements have completed by Friday.
The arrangements were completed by Friday.
questions.explanation: The future perfect passive is formed with 'will have been' plus the past participle 'completed'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Change to indirect speech: She said, 'I am tired.'
options: She said that I was tired.
She said that she is tired.
She said that she was tired.
questions.explanation: In reported speech, the present tense 'am' shifts back to the past tense 'was', and the pronoun changes to 'she'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Change to indirect speech: He said, 'I will call you tomorrow.'
options: He said I will call you tomorrow.
He said that he would call me tomorrow.
He said that he would call me the next day.
He said that he will call me tomorrow.
questions.explanation: 'Will' shifts to 'would' and 'tomorrow' becomes 'the next day' in reported speech.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Change to indirect speech: The teacher said, 'The earth revolves around the sun.'
options: The teacher said that the earth revolves around the sun.
The teacher said that earth revolves around sun.
The teacher said the earth will revolve around the sun.
The teacher said that the earth revolved around the sun.
questions.explanation: Universal truths and scientific facts remain in the present tense even in reported speech.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Change to indirect speech: She asked, 'Where do you live?'
options: She asked where do I live.
She asked me where did I live.
questions.explanation: In reported questions, the word order changes to a statement form and the auxiliary verb is dropped.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Change to indirect speech: He said, 'Please close the door.'
options: He said that close the door.
He requested me to close the door.
He said please close the door.
He asked did I close the door.
questions.explanation: Polite requests in reported speech are usually introduced with 'requested' or 'asked' followed by a to-infinitive.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Change to indirect speech: The doctor said, 'You must rest for a week.'
options: The doctor said you must rest for a week.
The doctor said that I must rest for a week.
The doctor said that I had to rest for a week.
The doctor said I must have rested for a week.
questions.explanation: The modal 'must' expressing obligation typically shifts to 'had to' in reported speech.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Change to indirect speech: They said, 'We have finished the project.'
options: They said that they had finished the project.
They said we finished the project.
They said that we have finished the project.
They said they have finished the project.
questions.explanation: The present perfect 'have finished' shifts back to the past perfect 'had finished' in reported speech.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Change to indirect speech: She said, 'I can swim very well.'
options: She said she can swims very well.
She said that she could swim very well.
She said that she can swim very well.
She said I could swim very well.
questions.explanation: The modal 'can' shifts back to 'could' in reported speech.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Change to indirect speech: He said to me, 'Did you see the accident?'
options: He asked if you saw the accident.
He asked me did you see the accident.
He asked me if I had seen the accident.
He asked me have I seen the accident.
questions.explanation: Yes/no questions in reported speech are introduced with 'if' or 'whether', and the tense shifts back.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Change to indirect speech: The manager said, 'I will complete the report by Friday.'
options: The manager said I will complete the report by Friday.
The manager said he completes the report by Friday.
The manager said that he would complete the report by Friday.
The manager said that he will complete the report by Friday.
questions.explanation: 'Will' shifts to 'would' in reported speech, and the pronoun changes accordingly.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Change to indirect speech: 'Do not touch the wire,' the electrician warned us.
options: The electrician warned us do not touch the wire.
The electrician warned us not to touch the wire.
The electrician warned that not touch the wire.
The electrician said do not touch the wire.
questions.explanation: Negative commands are reported using 'not to' plus the base verb.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Change to indirect speech: She said, 'What a beautiful dress this is!'
options: She said the dress is beautiful very.
She exclaimed what a beautiful dress it was.
She said what a beautiful dress this is.
She exclaimed that the dress was very beautiful.
questions.explanation: Exclamatory sentences are reported by expressing the sentiment in a statement, often introduced with 'exclaimed that'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Change to indirect speech: He said, 'Let us go to the market.'
options: He said let us go to the market.
He suggested that they go to the market.
He said that let us go to the market.
questions.explanation: Suggestions introduced by 'Let us' are reported using 'suggested that' plus a subjunctive verb form.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Change to indirect speech: The boy said, 'I am playing football now.'
options: The boy said he plays football now.
The boy said I am playing football now.
The boy said that he is playing football now.
The boy said that he was playing football then.
questions.explanation: The present continuous 'am playing' shifts to the past continuous 'was playing', and 'now' becomes 'then'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Change to indirect speech: 'I have never been to Europe,' she said.
options: She said that she had never been to Europe.
She said I have never been to Europe.
She said that she has never been to Europe.
She said she never went to Europe.
questions.explanation: The present perfect 'have never been' shifts to the past perfect 'had never been' in reported speech.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Change to indirect speech: 'Can you help me with this?' she asked him.
options: She asked if you could help her with that.
She asked him could you help me with this.
She asked him can you help me with this.
She asked him if he could help her with that.
questions.explanation: 'This' shifts to 'that' and 'can' shifts to 'could' when reporting the question.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Change to indirect speech: The chairman announced, 'The meeting will hold next Monday.'
options: The chairman announced that the meeting would hold the following Monday.
The chairman announced that the meeting will hold next Monday.
The chairman said the meeting held next Monday.
The chairman announced the meeting holds next Monday.
questions.explanation: 'Will' shifts to 'would' and 'next Monday' becomes 'the following Monday' in reported speech.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Change to indirect speech: 'I bought this dress yesterday,' she told her friend.
options: She told her friend she buys that dress yesterday.
She told her friend that she bought this dress yesterday.
She told her friend that she had bought that dress the day before.
She said I bought this dress yesterday.
questions.explanation: 'Bought' shifts to 'had bought', 'this' to 'that', and 'yesterday' to 'the day before'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Change to indirect speech: He asked, 'Why are you crying?'
options: He asked why are you crying.
He asked me why did I cry.
He asked why I was crying.
He asked why you were crying.
questions.explanation: In reported wh-questions, the word order becomes a statement and the tense shifts back.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Change to indirect speech: 'We shall overcome these challenges,' the leader declared.
options: The leader declared they overcame the challenges.
The leader declared that they would overcome those challenges.
The leader said we will overcome these challenges.
The leader declared that we shall overcome these challenges.
questions.explanation: 'Shall' shifts to 'would', 'we' to 'they', and 'these' to 'those' in reported speech.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Change to indirect speech: The coach said, 'Practice starts here tomorrow.'
options: The coach said that practice will start here.
The coach said that practice starts here tomorrow.
The coach said practice starts there tomorrow.
The coach said that practice started there the next day.
questions.explanation: 'Here' shifts to 'there', 'starts' to 'started', and 'tomorrow' to 'the next day' in reported speech.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Change to indirect speech: 'I must leave now,' she told them.
options: She said I must leave now.
She told them she must have left now.
She told them that she must leave now.
She told them that she had to leave then.
questions.explanation: The modal 'must' expressing obligation shifts to 'had to', and 'now' shifts to 'then' in reported speech.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Change to indirect speech: The inspector asked, 'Where were you last night?'
options: The inspector asked where were you last night.
The inspector asked where you were last night.
The inspector asked me where I was last night.
The inspector asked where I had been the previous night.
questions.explanation: The past tense 'were' shifts to the past perfect 'had been', and 'last night' becomes 'the previous night'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Change to indirect speech: 'Do you understand the instructions?' the officer asked the recruits.
options: The officer asked if you understand the instructions.
The officer asked the recruits did they understand instructions.
The officer asked the recruits do you understand the instructions.
The officer asked the recruits if they understood the instructions.
questions.explanation: Yes/no questions are reported using 'if', and the tense shifts back from present to past.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Change to indirect speech: 'I shall return next week,' he promised.
options: He promised he returns next week.
He said I shall return next week.
He promised that he would return the following week.
He promised that he shall return next week.
questions.explanation: 'Shall' shifts to 'would' and 'next week' becomes 'the following week' in reported speech.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correctly punctuated sentence.
options: We bought apples, oranges, and bananas.
We bought apples, oranges and, bananas.
We bought apples oranges, and bananas.
We bought, apples oranges and bananas.
questions.explanation: Commas are used to separate items in a list, including before the final conjunction (the Oxford comma).

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correctly punctuated sentence.
options: Although, it was raining, they continued the match.
Although it was raining they continued the match.
Although it was raining, they continued the match.
Although it was raining they, continued the match.
questions.explanation: A comma is used after an introductory subordinate clause that precedes the main clause.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the sentence with the correct use of the apostrophe.
options: The students books were left on the table
The students books' were left on the table.
The students' books were left on the table.
The student's books were left on the table.
questions.explanation: The apostrophe after the 's' in 'students'' shows plural possession, since the books belong to multiple students.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the sentence with the correct use of the semicolon.
options: She loves reading; he prefers watching movies.
She loves reading, he prefers watching movies.
She loves reading he prefers; watching movies.
She loves reading; he prefers, watching movies.
questions.explanation: A semicolon correctly joins two closely related independent clauses without a conjunction.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correctly punctuated sentence with a colon.
options: She needed: three things courage, patience, and time.
She needed three things: courage, patience, and time.
She needed three things, courage, patience, and time.
She needed three things: courage patience and time.
questions.explanation: A colon introduces a list that follows a complete independent clause.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the sentence with correctly placed quotation marks.
options: The teacher said, "Submit your assignments by Friday"
The teacher said, Submit your assignments by Friday.
The teacher said, "Submit your assignments by Friday."
The teacher said "Submit your assignments by Friday".
questions.explanation: Quotation marks enclose the exact words spoken, and the final punctuation goes inside the closing quotation mark.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correctly punctuated sentence using a comma to separate non-essential information.
options: My father who is a retired teacher, still tutors students.
My father, who is a retired teacher still tutors students.
My father who is a retired teacher still, tutors students.
My father, who is a retired teacher, still tutors students.
questions.explanation: Commas set off non-defining relative clauses that add extra, non-essential information.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the sentence that correctly uses a hyphen.
options: She gave a well-written-report to the board.
She gave a well, written report to the board.
She gave a well-written report to the board.
She gave a well written report to the board.
questions.explanation: A hyphen joins two words functioning together as a single compound adjective before a noun.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Which sentence correctly uses a question mark?
questions.explanation: A question mark is used at the end of a direct question.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correctly punctuated sentence with parentheses.
options: The workshop held last week) was very informative.
The workshop (held last week was very informative.
The workshop (held last week) was very informative.
The workshop, held last week, was very informative)
questions.explanation: Parentheses must open and close correctly around the additional information they enclose.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Which sentence correctly uses a comma before a coordinating conjunction joining two independent clauses?
options: She wanted to travel but, she had no money.
She wanted to travel, but, she had no money.
She wanted to travel, but she had no money.
She wanted to travel but she had no money,
questions.explanation: A comma is placed before the coordinating conjunction when it joins two independent clauses.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the sentence with the correct use of the apostrophe for a singular possessive noun.
options: The dogs bone was buried in the garden.
The dog' bone was buried in the garden.
The dog's bone was buried in the garden.
The dogs' bone was buried in the garden.
questions.explanation: For a singular noun, possession is shown by adding an apostrophe and 's': 'dog's'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correctly punctuated sentence using an exclamation mark.
options: What a wonderful performance that was!
What a wonderful performance that was.
What, a wonderful performance that was!
What a wonderful performance, that was!
questions.explanation: An exclamation mark is used to express strong emotion or surprise.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correctly punctuated sentence with a dash used for emphasis.
options: There was only one thing on her mind, success —
There was only one thing — on her mind success.
There was only one thing on her mind success —.
There was only one thing on her mind — success.
questions.explanation: A dash can be used to emphasise a word or phrase placed at the end of a sentence.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Which sentence correctly punctuates a direct address?
questions.explanation: A comma separates the name of the person being directly addressed from the rest of the sentence.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the sentence with the correct use of the apostrophe for a plural noun not ending in 's'.
options: The childrens' toys were scattered everywhere.
The children's toys were scattered everywhere.
The childrens toys were scattered everywhere.
The children toys' were scattered everywhere.
questions.explanation: For plural nouns that do not end in 's', such as 'children', possession is shown by adding an apostrophe and 's'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correctly punctuated sentence with an ellipsis showing a trailing thought.
options: I wanted to tell her, but,..
I wanted to tell her but...,
I wanted to tell her, but...
I wanted to tell her, but..
questions.explanation: An ellipsis of three dots is used to show a trailing or unfinished thought.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the sentence that correctly punctuates a list introduced within a sentence, without a colon.
options: Her favourite subjects were: English, Mathematics, and Biology.
Her favourite subjects were English, Mathematics, and Biology.
Her favourite subjects were English Mathematics and Biology.
Her favourite subjects were, English, Mathematics, and Biology.
questions.explanation: A colon should not be used when the list directly follows a verb like 'were' without a complete independent clause before it.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Which sentence correctly uses a comma to separate two adjectives of equal rank?
options: It was a long difficult, journey.
It was a long, difficult journey.
It was a long difficult journey,
It was a long, difficult, journey.
questions.explanation: A comma separates two coordinate adjectives of equal rank that both modify the same noun.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correctly punctuated sentence showing possession for a name ending in 's'.
options: Charless book was left on the desk.
Charles books was left on the desk.
Charles' book was left on the desk.
Charles's book was left on the desk.
questions.explanation: For most singular names ending in 's', possession is shown by adding an apostrophe and another 's': 'Charles's'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Which sentence correctly uses a comma after a conjunctive adverb?
options: The road was blocked; therefore, we took a different route.
The road was blocked, therefore, we took a different route.
The road was blocked; therefore. we took a different route.
The road was blocked; therefore we took a different route.
questions.explanation: A comma follows a conjunctive adverb like 'therefore' when it begins the second independent clause after a semicolon.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correctly punctuated sentence with a colon introducing a formal quotation.
options: The chairman began; "We are gathered here today."
The chairman began, We are gathered here today.
The chairman began "We are gathered here today":
The chairman began: "We are gathered here today."
questions.explanation: A colon can be used to formally introduce a direct quotation.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Which sentence correctly punctuates an interrupting phrase using dashes?
options: Her plan though risky — eventually — succeeded.
Her plan — though risky, eventually succeeded.
Her plan, though risky — eventually succeeded.
Her plan — though risky — eventually succeeded.
questions.explanation: A pair of dashes can enclose an interrupting phrase in the middle of a sentence, similar to commas or parentheses.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the sentence with the correct capitalisation and punctuation of a title.
options: She is reading Things fall Apart by chinua Achebe.
She is reading "Things Fall Apart" by Chinua Achebe.
She is reading "things fall apart" by Chinua Achebe.
She is reading things fall apart by chinua achebe.
questions.explanation: Titles of books are enclosed in quotation marks (or italicised) with each major word capitalised.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Which sentence correctly punctuates items in a series that themselves contain commas?
options: The winners were: John, first place; Mary, second place; and Musa, third place.
The winners were: John, first place, Mary, second place, and Musa, third place.
The winners were John first place, Mary second place, and Musa third place.
The winners were John, first place Mary, second place and Musa, third place.
questions.explanation: Semicolons are used to separate items in a list when the items themselves already contain commas.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correctly punctuated sentence showing joint possession by two people.
options: John's and Mary's house was renovated last year.
John and Mary's house was renovated last year.
Johns and Marys house was renovated last year.
John and Marys' house was renovated last year.
questions.explanation: When two people jointly own something, the apostrophe is added only to the last name: 'John and Mary's'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Which sentence correctly punctuates separate possession by two people?
options: Johns and Marys opinions differed greatly.
John's and Mary's opinions on the matter differed greatly.
John and Mary's opinions on the matter differed greatly.
John's and Marys opinions differed greatly.
questions.explanation: When two people possess separate things, each name takes its own apostrophe and 's': 'John's and Mary's'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the sentence that correctly uses a comma to set off an introductory phrase.
options: After the long meeting everyone went home, exhausted.
After the long meeting everyone, went home exhausted.
After, the long meeting, everyone went home exhausted.
After the long meeting, everyone went home exhausted.
questions.explanation: A comma follows an introductory phrase that comes before the main clause.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Which sentence correctly avoids a comma splice?
options: She finished her work; then she went home.
She finished her work then, she went home.
She finished her work, then, she went home.
She finished her work, then she went home.
questions.explanation: A semicolon (not a comma) is needed to correctly join two independent clauses without a coordinating conjunction, avoiding a comma splice.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the sentence that correctly uses brackets to insert an editorial clarification into a quotation.
options: "He [the governor] promised to fix the roads," the newspaper reported.
"He (the governor) promised to fix the roads", the newspaper reported.
"He the governor promised to fix the roads," the newspaper reported.
"He [the governor promised] to fix the roads," the newspaper reported.
questions.explanation: Square brackets are used within a quotation to insert a clarifying word that was not part of the original speech.

questions.text:
When Ngozi's father lost his job at the textile factory, the family's fortunes changed almost overnight. Gone were the weekend outings to the cinema; gone too was the extra plate of meat at dinner. Ngozi, then in her final year of secondary school, watched her mother take up petty trading to keep the household afloat, rising before dawn to fry akara by the roadside. Rather than sink into despair, Ngozi resolved that her family's hardship would be the fuel, not the flame, that consumed her ambitions. She studied by candlelight when the electricity failed, borrowed textbooks from wealthier classmates, and tutored younger pupils for a small fee to contribute to the family's income. When the results of the West African Senior School Certificate Examination were released, Ngozi had distinctions in eight subjects — a feat that stunned even her teachers. Her story, whispered admiringly around the school compound, became a quiet rebuke to anyone who believed that poverty was an excuse for mediocrity.

According to the passage, what event changed the fortunes of Ngozi's family?
questions.explanation: The passage opens by stating that the father's job loss at the textile factory changed the family's fortunes.

Ngozi, then in her final year of secondary school, watched her mother take up petty trading to keep the household afloat, rising before dawn to fry akara by the roadside. Rather than sink into despair, Ngozi resolved that her family's hardship would be the fuel, not the flame, that consumed her ambitions. She studied by candlelight when the electricity failed, borrowed textbooks from wealthier classmates, and tutored younger pupils for a small fee to contribute to the family's income. When the results of the West African Senior School Certificate Examination were released, Ngozi had distinctions in eight subjects — a feat that stunned even her teachers. Her story, whispered admiringly around the school compound, became a quiet rebuke to anyone who believed that poverty was an excuse for mediocrity.

What did Ngozi's mother do to support the household?
options: She took up petty trading, frying akara
She asked relatives for a loan
questions.explanation: The passage states the mother took up petty trading, rising before dawn to fry akara by the roadside.

questions.text:
The rapid spread of smartphones across rural Nigeria has quietly transformed the way farmers conduct business. A decade ago, a maize farmer in a remote village had to rely on middlemen to learn the going price of grain in distant urban markets, a arrangement that often left him at the mercy of unscrupulous traders. Today, that same farmer can consult a mobile application, compare prices across three states, and negotiate from a position of knowledge rather than ignorance. Agricultural extension officers have also embraced the technology, sending voice notes in local languages to warn of impending pest outbreaks or advise on planting seasons. Yet the revolution remains incomplete. Many villages still lack reliable network coverage, and older farmers, unfamiliar with touchscreens, often depend on their literate grandchildren to operate the very devices meant to empower them. Bridging this final gap, analysts argue, will determine whether the digital transformation of agriculture becomes a genuine leveller or merely another advantage reserved for the already privileged.

According to the passage, what problem did farmers face a decade ago?
options: They had no access to fertile land
They had to rely on middlemen for price information
They could not grow maize successfully
questions.explanation: The passage states farmers relied on middlemen to learn grain prices in distant markets.

Few sporting rivalries in West Africa stir as much passion as the annual inter-secondary schools athletics championship held in the capital. Students who have trained for months on dusty school fields descend upon the stadium, their school colours fluttering like a thousand competing flags. Last year's final one hundred metre race will long be remembered, not for the eventual winner, but for a moment of extraordinary sportsmanship. Halfway through the race, the front-runner, sensing that a rival behind him had stumbled and fallen, slowed his own stride, turned back, and helped the fallen boy to his feet before both resumed running. Neither finished among the medal positions, yet the crowd rose as one, applauding a display of character that no trophy could adequately reward. The incident, captured on countless phone cameras, spread quickly across social media, prompting the sports ministry to introduce a new fair play award, to be presented annually alongside the conventional medals for speed and strength.

According to the passage, where is the inter-secondary schools athletics championship held?
questions.explanation: The passage states the championship is held annually in the capital.

Few sporting rivalries in West Africa stir as much passion as the annual inter-secondary schools athletics championship held in the capital. Students who have trained for months on dusty school fields descend upon the stadium, their school colours fluttering like a thousand competing flags. Last year's final one hundred metre race will long be remembered, not for the eventual winner, but for a moment of extraordinary sportsmanship. Halfway through the race, the front-runner, sensing that a rival behind him had stumbled and fallen, slowed his own stride, turned back, and helped the fallen boy to his feet before both resumed running. Neither finished among the medal positions, yet the crowd rose as one, applauding a display of character that no trophy could adequately reward. The incident, captured on countless phone cameras, spread quickly across social media, prompting the sports ministry to introduce a new fair play award, to be presented annually alongside the conventional medals for speed and strength.

In many Nigerian households, the extended family system functions as an informal social security network, quietly absorbing shocks that would otherwise devastate a nuclear family. When Uncle Tunde's small business collapsed during the economic downturn, it was his brothers and cousins, rather than any government agency, who pooled resources to keep his children in school. Sociologists have long debated whether this arrangement is a strength or a burden. Proponents argue that it fosters resilience, spreading risk across dozens of shoulders rather than concentrating it on two overworked parents. Critics counter that the system can breed resentment, as the more financially successful members of a family are perpetually expected to subsidise relatives who make little effort to improve their own circumstances. Whatever one's view, the extended family shows no sign of disappearing; if anything, the retreat of the state from social welfare provision in recent decades has only deepened society's reliance on this ancient, unwritten contract between kin.

According to the passage, what happened to Uncle Tunde's business?
options: It was taken over by the government
It collapsed during the economic downturn
It was sold to a competitor
questions.explanation: The passage states Uncle Tunde's small business collapsed during the economic downturn.

questions.text:
The abandoned railway line that once connected the northern city to the coast is, for most travellers, little more than a rusting curiosity glimpsed from a bus window. Yet for a small but determined group of railway enthusiasts, it represents a lost golden age of national infrastructure. Built during the colonial era to transport groundnuts and cotton to the ports, the railway carried not just cargo but also generations of students, traders, and civil servants who could not otherwise have afforded to travel such distances. Its gradual decline, beginning in the 1980s as road transport became cheaper and more flexible, mirrors a broader pattern across the continent, where ambitious colonial-era rail networks were left to decay rather than modernised. Recently, however, renewed interest from foreign investors, eager to move minerals more efficiently than congested roads allow, has breathed fresh hope into plans for restoration. Whether this hope translates into steel and concrete, or remains another unfulfilled promise in a long list of abandoned proposals, only time will tell.

According to the passage, what was the railway originally built to transport, aside from passengers?
questions.explanation: The passage states the railway was built to transport groundnuts and cotton to the ports.

Doctor Amara had seen countless cases of malaria during her years at the rural clinic, but nothing had prepared her for the outbreak that swept through the fishing community that rainy season. Stagnant pools left by the flooding had become breeding grounds for mosquitoes, and within weeks, the clinic's twelve beds were hopelessly insufficient for the flood of feverish patients. Working with little more than a handful of volunteers and a dwindling stock of medication, she improvised a triage system on the veranda, prioritising children and pregnant women whose lives hung most precariously in the balance. News of the crisis eventually reached the state ministry of health, and reinforcements arrived, but not before three lives had already been lost. In the aftermath, Doctor Amara campaigned tirelessly for a permanent drainage system in the community, arguing that treating the disease without addressing its environmental cause was like mopping a floor while the tap kept running. Her advocacy eventually bore fruit; two years later, a functioning drainage network reduced malaria cases in the community by more than half.

According to the passage, what caused the malaria outbreak in the fishing community?
options: Stagnant pools from flooding became mosquito breeding grounds
questions.explanation: The passage states stagnant pools left by flooding became breeding grounds for mosquitoes.

questions.text:
Doctor Amara had seen countless cases of malaria during her years at the rural clinic, but nothing had prepared her for the outbreak that swept through the fishing community that rainy season. Stagnant pools left by the flooding had become breeding grounds for mosquitoes, and within weeks, the clinic's twelve beds were hopelessly insufficient for the flood of feverish patients. Working with little more than a handful of volunteers and a dwindling stock of medication, she improvised a triage system on the veranda, prioritising children and pregnant women whose lives hung most precariously in the balance. News of the crisis eventually reached the state ministry of health, and reinforcements arrived, but not before three lives had already been lost. In the aftermath, Doctor Amara campaigned tirelessly for a permanent drainage system in the community, arguing that treating the disease without addressing its environmental cause was like mopping a floor while the tap kept running. Her advocacy eventually bore fruit; two years later, a functioning drainage network reduced malaria cases in the community by more than half.

Which of the following best captures the main idea of the passage?
options: The clinic had more than enough resources for the outbreak
Government reinforcements arrived before any lives were lost
Malaria cannot be prevented through infrastructure
Addressing the root cause of a health crisis proved more effective than treating symptoms alone
questions.explanation: The passage highlights how tackling the environmental cause (stagnant water) through drainage ultimately reduced malaria cases.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
It is easy, from the comfort of a well-lit office, to romanticise the life of a long-distance truck driver hauling goods across the trans-Saharan trade route. The reality, as any veteran driver will attest, is a gruelling test of endurance measured in cracked windscreens, sleepless nights, and the ever-present risk of armed robbery on isolated stretches of highway. Alhaji Musa has driven this route for over twenty years, ferrying everything from bags of rice to secondhand car parts between the coast and the interior. He speaks of the job not with romantic nostalgia but with the weary pragmatism of a man who has simply found no better alternative to feed his family. The introduction of GPS tracking and mobile banking has eased some burdens, allowing drivers to alert their companies instantly in emergencies and receive payment without carrying dangerous amounts of cash. Yet the fundamental hazards of the road, from potholes the size of small ponds to checkpoints manned by officials seeking bribes, remain stubbornly unchanged, a reminder that technology alone cannot repair what decades of poor infrastructure investment have broken.

According to the passage, how long has Alhaji Musa driven the trans-Saharan route?
questions.explanation: The passage states Alhaji Musa has driven this route for over twenty years.

questions.text:
The debate over whether social media has been a net positive or negative for Nigerian youth shows no sign of resolution. Advocates point to the democratisation of information: a teenager in a remote village can now access lectures from world-renowned universities, follow breaking news as it unfolds, and even build a small business selling handmade crafts to customers thousands of kilometres away. Critics, meanwhile, warn of the corrosive effects of constant comparison, as curated images of wealth and beauty foster anxiety and discontent among impressionable minds. Mental health professionals report a marked increase in young patients citing social media as a contributing factor to their distress, though establishing a direct causal link remains scientifically contentious. Perhaps the most honest conclusion is that social media, like fire, is neither inherently good nor evil; its ultimate effect depends entirely on how it is wielded, and by whom. Parents, educators, and policymakers alike are still groping for the right balance between harnessing its benefits and shielding young minds from its more corrosive tendencies.

According to the passage, what benefit of social media do advocates highlight?
options: Complete elimination of mental health issues
Guaranteed financial wealth for all users
Access to educational content and business opportunities
questions.explanation: The passage states advocates point to access to university lectures, breaking news, and building small businesses.

questions.text:
The city council's decision to convert an abandoned industrial site into a public park was met with scepticism by residents who had grown accustomed to years of empty promises. For nearly a decade, the derelict warehouse had served as an unofficial dumping ground, its rusting hulk a magnet for scrap metal thieves and stray dogs. Community organiser Blessing Eze recalls the first town hall meeting on the proposal, where elderly attendees openly laughed at officials, having heard similar pledges made and abandoned by three previous administrations. Yet this time, something was different. A coalition of youth volunteers, armed with little more than wheelbarrows and stubborn optimism, began clearing debris every Saturday morning, refusing to wait for government machinery that might never arrive. Their visible progress shamed the council into action, accelerating budget approvals that might otherwise have languished for years. Eighteen months later, children who had never known anything but broken glass and weeds now play football on a patch of grass their grandparents once thought impossible.

According to the passage, what had the derelict warehouse become before the park project began?
questions.explanation: The passage states the warehouse had served as an unofficial dumping ground for nearly a decade.

Chief Okonjo's decision to send all four of his daughters to university, at a time when many of his peers considered such an investment wasted on girls destined for marriage, was regarded in the village as either visionary or reckless, depending on whom one asked. He had little formal education himself, having left school after primary six to help on the family farm, and he often said that his own limitations were precisely why he refused to impose them on his children. His eldest daughter now practises medicine in the state capital; the second manages a thriving textile business; the third teaches physics to secondary school students; and the youngest, still in her final year, hopes to become an engineer. Neighbours who once whispered that Chief Okonjo was squandering his modest savings on daughters who would simply marry and leave now send their own daughters to ask his advice. He accepts the belated praise with characteristic modesty, insisting that he merely refused to let tradition dictate the limits of what his children could achieve.

options: Arrange marriages for all of them

Send only the eldest to school
Send all four of them to university
questions.explanation: The passage states he decided to send all four of his daughters to university.

questions.text:
Few natural phenomena capture the imagination quite like the harmattan, the dry, dust-laden wind that sweeps down from the Sahara each year, coating rooftops in a fine ochre film and turning the sky a hazy grey-brown for weeks on end. For children in many parts of West Africa, the harmattan season carries a peculiar magic: school mornings so cold that breath fogs in the air, followed by afternoons where the same dust that irritates throats and cracks lips also produces spectacular sunsets, the sun reduced to a dull orange disc one can stare at directly. Farmers view the season with more ambivalence, welcoming the dry conditions that ease harvesting but dreading the moisture the parched air steals from their remaining crops. Meteorologists, meanwhile, study the harmattan's intensity as an indicator of the coming rainy season, with an unusually fierce harmattan often, though not always reliably, preceding heavier rains. Whatever one's perspective, the harmattan remains an unshakeable fixture of the regional calendar, as certain and as commented upon as the changing of the seasons anywhere else in the world.

According to the passage, where does the harmattan wind originate?
questions.explanation: The passage states the harmattan sweeps down from the Sahara each year.

When the government first announced plans to phase out the popular but heavily polluting two-stroke motorcycle taxis, known locally as okada, from the city centre, the reaction from riders was swift and furious. For tens of thousands of young men, many of whom had abandoned fruitless searches for formal employment, the okada represented not just a job but a fragile foothold on economic dignity. Protests shut down major roads for three consecutive days, forcing the transport ministry back to the negotiating table. The eventual compromise, brokered after weeks of tense discussion, allowed riders to convert their two-stroke engines to cleaner four-stroke alternatives at a heavily subsidised cost, spreading payments over eighteen months. Environmental campaigners grumbled that the deal was too generous to an industry they blamed for choking the city with exhaust fumes, while riders' associations complained that even subsidised conversion costs remained beyond the reach of the poorest operators. The policy, imperfect as it was, nonetheless demonstrated that even the most entrenched conflicts between economic survival and environmental necessity could yield to patient, if imperfect, negotiation.

The old woman who sells roasted corn beneath the flame tree at the junction has become, without ever intending it, an unofficial historian of the neighbourhood. Ask her about the year the floods reached the mosque steps, or which family first owned the plot where the new supermarket now stands, and she will recount the details with the precision of someone reading from a ledger, though she has never learned to read at all. Her memory, honed by decades of listening to the gossip and grievances exchanged over her charcoal brazier, has become a resource that no municipal archive can rival. Urban planners, oddly enough, have begun to seek her out when disputes arise over land boundaries, since her recollections of who built what fence, and when, often settle arguments that official documents, lost or falsified over the years, cannot. She finds this newfound relevance amusing, remarking with a wry smile that after seventy years of being overlooked, it is strange to suddenly matter to men in suits who once would not have glanced twice at a corn seller.

According to the passage, what does the old woman sell?
questions.explanation: The passage states she sells roasted corn beneath the flame tree at the junction.

Nobody in the small coastal town expected the annual canoe regatta to attract international attention, least of all the fishermen who had organised it for generations as little more than a friendly test of strength and skill after the fishing season ended. Yet when a documentary crew, drawn initially by unrelated stories of coastal erosion, happened to film the colourful, chaotic spectacle of forty hand-carved canoes racing through the surf, the footage went unexpectedly viral online. Within months, a tourism board that had never previously acknowledged the town's existence was funding improved facilities, and hotels that once struggled to fill a handful of rooms found themselves fully booked during regatta season. The fishermen, initially bemused by the sudden influx of camera-wielding visitors, have since organised themselves into an association to negotiate fairer terms with tour operators, determined that outsiders profiting from their tradition would not do so at the expense of the community that had sustained it for so long.

According to the passage, why was the canoe regatta originally organised?
options: As a friendly test of strength and skill after the fishing season
To raise funds for the town council
questions.explanation: The passage states fishermen organised it for generations as a friendly test of strength and skill after the fishing season ended.

Nobody in the small coastal town expected the annual canoe regatta to attract international attention, least of all the fishermen who had organised it for generations as little more than a friendly test of strength and skill after the fishing season ended. Yet when a documentary crew, drawn initially by unrelated stories of coastal erosion, happened to film the colourful, chaotic spectacle of forty hand-carved canoes racing through the surf, the footage went unexpectedly viral online. Within months, a tourism board that had never previously acknowledged the town's existence was funding improved facilities, and hotels that once struggled to fill a handful of rooms found themselves fully booked during regatta season. The fishermen, initially bemused by the sudden influx of camera-wielding visitors, have since organised themselves into an association to negotiate fairer terms with tour operators, determined that outsiders profiting from their tradition would not do so at the expense of the community that had sustained it for so long.

In the context of the passage, the word 'bemused' is nearest in meaning to:
questions.explanation: 'Bemused' describes a state of mild confusion or puzzlement, here referring to the fishermen's reaction to sudden attention.

questions.text:
The controversy surrounding the proposed dam project pits two seemingly incompatible visions of progress against one another. Supporters, chiefly government engineers and energy companies, point to the dam's potential to triple the region's electricity generation, finally ending the rolling blackouts that have throttled small businesses for a generation. Opponents, drawn largely from the fishing communities that would be displaced by the reservoir, argue that the promised electricity has, in similar past projects elsewhere, rarely reached the very villages sacrificed for its generation, flowing instead to distant cities and industrial estates. Independent environmental assessors have added a further complication, warning that the dam could disrupt fish migration patterns that thousands of downstream families depend upon for their livelihoods, a concern the project's engineers dismiss as manageable through unproven mitigation technology. As construction machinery sits idle awaiting a final court ruling, the dam has become a proxy battle for a larger, unresolved national question: who bears the cost of progress, and who reaps its rewards?

According to the passage, what benefit do supporters of the dam project claim it will bring?
questions.explanation: The passage states supporters point to the dam's potential to triple the region's electricity generation.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
There is a particular kind of quiet heroism in the work of the community health volunteers who trek for hours along bush paths to deliver vaccines to villages too remote for any tarred road to reach. Mama Ijeoma, sixty-one years old and a volunteer for over two decades, carries a cool box strapped to her back containing vaccines that must remain within a strict temperature range or spoil entirely, rendering an already arduous journey worthless. She has waded through swollen streams during the rainy season and walked for six hours under a punishing sun during the dry months, motivated by nothing more than a modest stipend and an unshakeable conviction that no child's survival should depend on the accident of where they happen to be born. Public health statistics, dry and impersonal as they often are, rarely capture the individual toll of such journeys, yet it is precisely volunteers like Mama Ijeoma who have quietly driven down child mortality rates in areas that formal healthcare infrastructure has been slow, or unable, to reach.

According to the passage, what does Mama Ijeoma carry on her journeys?
questions.explanation: The passage states she carries a cool box strapped to her back containing vaccines.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
The renovation of the century-old central market was meant to be a straightforward exercise in modernisation: new roofing to replace the leaking asbestos sheets, proper drainage to end the seasonal flooding that ruined perishable goods, and designated parking to ease the chaotic congestion of delivery trucks. Instead, it became a protracted battle over identity and memory. Traders whose grandparents had occupied the same stalls for three generations resisted the council's plan to reorganise vendors by category rather than by the informal, decades-old arrangements everyone had simply inherited. To an outside consultant, the proposed changes seemed purely logistical, a sensible way to help customers navigate the market more efficiently. To the traders, however, their stall's specific location was inseparable from their family's history and reputation, built painstakingly over decades of loyal customers finding them in exactly the same spot. The eventual compromise preserved most traditional stall locations while introducing the promised infrastructure improvements, proving that successful modernisation sometimes requires bending to sentiment rather than insisting on pure efficiency.

According to the passage, what infrastructure improvements were originally planned for the market?
options: New roofing, drainage, and designated parking
questions.explanation: The passage states plans included new roofing, proper drainage, and designated parking.

It is tempting to view the recent surge in youth entrepreneurship purely as an inspiring story of innovation and grit, but a closer look reveals a more complicated picture. Many of the young people launching small businesses, from mobile phone repair kiosks to social media marketing agencies, are doing so not out of burning entrepreneurial passion but because formal employment opportunities have simply failed to materialise in sufficient numbers for a rapidly growing, increasingly educated population. Necessity, rather than inspiration, is frequently the true engine of this entrepreneurial boom. This distinction matters for policy: programmes designed to celebrate and fund visionary innovators may do little for the vast majority of young entrepreneurs who would happily abandon their small enterprises the moment a stable salaried position became available. What this cohort needs is not motivational seminars about risk-taking, but practical support, affordable credit, reliable electricity, and simplified business registration, that allows their necessity-driven ventures to survive long enough to become something more permanent and, perhaps eventually, genuinely chosen rather than merely endured.

According to the passage, what is often the true motivation behind youth entrepreneurship?
options: A desire to avoid all forms of work
Necessity, due to a lack of formal employment opportunities
questions.explanation: The passage states necessity, rather than inspiration, is frequently the true engine of the entrepreneurial boom.

Grandfather's old transistor radio, held together at this point more by tape and stubbornness than by any remaining original casing, occupies a place of honour on the sitting room shelf despite the family owning three modern smart speakers that could easily replace its function. Ask him why he refuses to discard it, and he will tell you, with the patience of a man who has explained this many times before, that the radio carried him through the loneliest years of his life as a young migrant labourer in a foreign city, its crackling broadcasts of home-language news and music the only thread connecting him to a country he feared he might never see again. The smart speakers, for all their crisp digital clarity, cannot replicate the specific static hiss that, to him, sounds unmistakably like comfort. His grandchildren tease him gently about his sentimental attachment to what they consider obsolete junk, but even they have noticed that he seems to sit a little straighter, a little more present, whenever the old radio's dial catches a distant, half-audible signal on a quiet evening.

questions.explanation: The passage states the family owns three modern smart speakers that could easily replace the radio's function.

The smart speakers, for all their crisp digital clarity, cannot replicate the specific static hiss that, to him, sounds unmistakably like comfort. His grandchildren tease him gently about his sentimental attachment to what they consider obsolete junk, but even they have noticed that he seems to sit a little straighter, a little more present, whenever the old radio's dial catches a distant, half-audible signal on a quiet evening.

Which of the following best captures the main idea of the passage?
options: Grandfather refuses to accept any new technology in his home
Modern technology is always superior to old devices
An old object's value can lie in emotional memory rather than practical function
The grandchildren fully understand and share his attachment to the radio
questions.explanation: The passage illustrates how Grandfather's attachment to the radio stems from emotional significance rather than its technical usefulness.

questions.text:
The apprenticeship system practised among the Igbo trading community, known as Igba Boi, has quietly produced more small business owners than any single government entrepreneurship programme, though it rarely receives comparable academic or media attention. Under this arrangement, a young man works for an established trader, typically for five to seven years, receiving accommodation, feeding, and practical business training in exchange for his labour, but no direct salary. At the conclusion of this period, provided his service has been satisfactory, his master provides him with capital, sometimes substantial, to establish his own independent business, often in the same trade. Critics point out the system's vulnerability to exploitation, noting cases where masters extend the apprenticeship indefinitely or dismiss apprentices shortly before settlement to avoid payment. Defenders counter that such abuses, while real, represent a minority of cases, and that the system's overall track record of transforming penniless young men into self-sufficient business owners, without requiring any government subsidy or formal collateral, remains remarkable by any measure of economic development.

According to the passage, what does the Igba Boi apprenticeship system typically involve?
options: A young man working for an established trader for five to seven years
Government-funded business training for one year
University education followed by an internship
A short trial period of a few weeks
questions.explanation: The passage states a young man works for an established trader, typically for five to seven years.
